draft.title: Benchmarking
card: Benchmarking is comparing a business's results with a standard. The standard might be a competitor, the industry average or the best business in the field.
The business picks a measure, such as the cost of making each item or the time taken to serve a customer. It then compares its own figure with the benchmark.
A gap shows where the business is behind. The business can then look at how the better performer works and change its own methods to close the gap.
The standard comes from outside the business. This is different from checking results against the business's own plan.
draft.remember: Benchmarking compares results with an outside standard to find ways to improve.

a.q: Which action is an example of benchmarking?
opts: A bakery compares its cost per loaf with the industry average
A bakery checks its sales against its own monthly target
A bakery asks staff to suggest ideas for new bread flavours
A bakery plans what to do if its oven breaks down
a.why: The bakery compares its own cost with an outside standard, the industry average, to see where it can improve. Checking sales against its own target is not benchmarking, because the standard is the business's own plan, not an outside one.
a.clue: Look for a comparison with a standard from outside the business.

b.q: Priya runs a gym in Ballarat. She finds that a rival gym signs up new members in half the time hers takes. What should she do to benchmark?
opts: Study how the rival signs up members and change her process
Cut her prices so that she has more members than the rival
Check her sign-up times against the targets in her own plan
Wait to see whether her sign-up times improve by themselves
b.why: Benchmarking uses the gap with a better performer to find ways to improve, so Priya should study how the rival works and adjust her own process. Comparing with her own plan's targets is tempting, but that standard is internal, not an outside benchmark.
b.clue: The aim is to learn from the business that does it better.
